before.label: Historical demography & history of the family
before.description: Combines related inquiries into population, households, childhood and intimate relations. Henry’s family reconstitution and Cambridge’s aggregate and household studies differ from Ariès’s historical concepts and Stone’s family interpretation. Pollock’s criticism questions evidence and sweeping changes in parental care. Lee and Wang’s Chinese population study challenges received Malthusian comparisons without making the field’s regional patterns uniform.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Louis Henry; Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure (1964); Peter Laslett, The World We Have Lost (1965); Wrigley and Schofield, The Population History of England (1981); Philippe Ariès (1960); Lawrence Stone (1977). Additional selections: Hajnal (1965); Laslett and Wall (1972); Pollock (1981/1983); Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield (1997); Lee and Wang (1999).

before.scope_note: Family reconstitution and aggregate reconstruction differ from histories of childhood or family meanings; Henry, Annales, and Cambridge are not interchangeable. Household composition, marriage behavior, concepts of childhood and parental conduct are different objects of study. England and France are prominent in this selection; Chinese comparative research broadens the questions without representing all non-European family histories. Later institutional webpages are retrospective sources, not an extension beyond 2000.

strands.title: Reconstituting families from historical records
strands.focus: Link records of family events while examining who disappears from observation; Henry flags mobility and social differences, and Cambridge’s 1997 study is explicitly collaborative.
strands.works: Anciennes familles genevoises (1956); English Population History from Family Reconstitution (1997)

strands.title: Reconstructing aggregate population
strands.focus: Use historical demographic observations to estimate population and vital rates; a national reconstruction is distinct from following the observed life of one family.
strands.works: The Population History of England 1541–1871: A Reconstruction (1981)

strands.title: Households and comparative marriage patterns
strands.focus: Compare household composition and marriage patterns without inferring feelings from household size or treating one region as universal.
strands.works: Household and Family in Past Time (1972); “European Marriage Patterns in Perspective” (1965)

strands.title: Childhood concepts, conduct and evidence
strands.focus: Ariès examines childhood as a historical concept; Pollock questions broad change narratives through personal documents. Affection and recognition of a separate life stage are not identical claims.
strands.works: Centuries of Childhood (1962); The Forgotten Children (1981); Forgotten Children (1983)

strands.title: Marriage, intimacy and disputed change
strands.focus: Stone’s affective-individualism interpretation meets criticism of its explanation and evidential selection. Neither prescriptive literature nor diary writers transparently represent everyone.
strands.works: The Family, Sex and Marriage in England (1977); Pollock’s thesis, pp. 96–98 and 143–144 (1981)

strands.title: Chinese population and Malthusian comparisons
strands.focus: Lee and Wang argue for forms of population regulation missed by received China/West contrasts. Their fertility and marriage claims remain arguments to test against evidence and regional variation.
strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999)

strands.title: Patterns, exceptions and explanation
strands.focus: Hajnal distinguishes late marriage from remaining unmarried, acknowledges regional variation and separates identifying a pattern from explaining it. Goody questions its uniqueness and the scale of comparison.

strands.title: Local monographs and collective sampling
strands.focus: Fleury and Henry credit Goubert and other researchers, but argue that chosen parish monographs cannot simply be added into a national sample. Biraben joins their subsequent register inventory.
strands.works: Fleury/Henry (1958),665; Biraben/Fleury/Henry (1960), metadata

strands.title: Population totals and family subsets
strands.focus: Henry’s survey account distinguishes aggregate reconstruction from the smaller rural sample used for family reconstitution. Changes in sampling and uneven record quality constrain what each can establish.
strands.works: INED survey account (1978),230–232

strands.title: Observed fertility and deliberate control
strands.focus: Lee and Wang interpret delayed first births, longer intervals and earlier stopping as marital restraint. Harrell’s later review questions source completeness, regional reach and whether these patterns establish intentional control.
strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999),86–90; Harrell review (2003),543

strands.title: Local evidence and collaborative reconstruction
strands.focus: Harrell’s collection brings local demographic studies together; Lee and Wang acknowledge Campbell’s contributions. A broad comparative argument still requires attention to differences among local sources.
strands.works: Chinese Historical Microdemography (1995); One Quarter of Humanity (1999), opening acknowledgment

strands.title: Family change, social differences and source selection
strands.focus: Stone qualifies affective individualism with reversals and overlapping patterns across social groups, while making a debatable assumption about surviving documents. Pollock separates childhood concepts, affection and discipline and questions how family histories generalize from their sources.
strands.works: Stone, abridged edition (1979), 21–29; Pollock, Forgotten Children (1983), 1–10

strands.title: Italian residence and marriage patterns
strands.focus: Kertzer and Hogan report patrilocal residence without the expected combination of early female marriage, large spousal age differences and low nonmarriage. Similar marriage ages among wage workers and sharecroppers complicate a simple account of proletarianization.
strands.works: “Reflections on the European Marriage Pattern” (1991), Casalecchio, 1861–1921

added.citation: Lawrence Stone, The Family, Sex and Marriage in England, 1500–1800, abridged edition (Harper & Row, 1979), 21–29.

verification.note: Primary title/imprint and printed 21–29 read through local OCR; imprint visually checked. First Harper paperback 1979, copyright 1977/1979; distinct from the existing 1977 record. Pages 22–24 qualify change by reversals, social strata and overlapping family types; 25 assumes surviving personal documents broadly representative despite intimate material destroyed; 26–27 acknowledge literate-minority bias and difficulties selecting representative cases. Remaining scan and original records unread; the author’s representativeness assumption is not independently validated.

added.title: David I. Kertzer and Dennis P. Hogan, “Reflections on the European Marriage Pattern: Sharecropping and Proletarianization in Casalecchio, Italy, 1861–1921,” Journal of Family History 16.1 (1991), 31–45.
added.citation: David I. Kertzer and Dennis P. Hogan, “Reflections on the European Marriage Pattern: Sharecropping and Proletarianization in Casalecchio, Italy, 1861–1921,” Journal of Family History 16.1 (1991), 31–45.

verification.note: Complete official research abstract and bibliographic record read. Reports a Casalecchio challenge to Hajnal/Laslett classifications and simple industrialization–marriage-age associations. Author bibliography https://www.davidkertzer.com/articles corroborates authorship and pages. Article PDF returned 403 both normally and with authorized escalation; full argument, tables and underlying records unread. A substantive author-reported local result, not independent numerical replication or a claim about all Italy.

verification.note: Publisher excerpt printed 1–10 read via OCR at https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/401759/9780521271332_excerpt_001.pdf ; pages 2 and 10 visually collated. Page 2 separates Ariès’s childhood concept from ill-treatment and later writers’ claims about parental formality. Pages 6–9 question generalization from public policy, a royal child and secondary accounts; page 10 records Stone’s fluctuating discipline alongside his claim of increasing concern. Excerpt ends during the literature review; Pollock’s own diary-analysis chapters and endnotes unread. Prior metadata retained in history. The separately checked 1981 thesis is not treated as identical to the 1983 book; Stone’s independently read 1979 abridgment has its own source record.

outcomes.finding: Pollock’s 1983 opening literature review distinguishes childhood concepts from ill-treatment and parental formality; it also records Stone’s fluctuating discipline. Stone’s independently read 1979 abridgment qualifies affective individualism by social strata, overlapping types and reversals while making contestable source-representativeness assumptions. Kertzer and Hogan’s Casalecchio findings add a substantive Italian case challenging the association of residence with marriage age and simple proletarianization models.
outcomes.research_limit: Pollock 1–10 only, with 2 and 10 visually collated; diary-analysis chapters and endnotes unread. The 1981 thesis remains separate. Stone 1979 abridgment title/imprint and 21–29 read, not the entire book or 1977 unabridged text. Kertzer/Hogan complete official research abstract and metadata only; PDF returned 403 normally and with authorized escalation. Neither original records nor numerical results independently audited; local Italian case does not represent all Italy.
